problem: VLM-based VLN navigators such as StreamVLN and NaVIDA reach strong benchmark scores, but on real robots they move stop-and-go. The runtime is a blocking sense→inference→execution loop, so the controller idles while each new observation is sensed, transmitted and processed. Making action generation faster does not remove this structural waiting.
motivation: On a Unitree G1 running native NaVIDA with a remote RTX 5090 server, the controller waits 10.64 s per episode on average. That is a 30.5% waiting ratio, with 9.25 pauses over 9.75 inference rounds, so 94.9% of rounds are stop-and-go. The visible gap (1.09 s) nearly equals the inference round trip (0.97 s). The bottleneck is therefore how latency is exposed to the controller, not policy quality. Continuity should be treated as a first-class deployment metric.
key_idea: Wrap a frozen multi-step VLM navigator in a dual-thread runtime. One thread keeps executing a short committed 'guard buffer' while the other refreshes the continuation from the newest observation. The guard is sized in wall-clock time to just cover the next inference latency, and the rest of the continuation stays as a revisable tail that the refresh can overwrite.
insight: Hiding latency requires overlapping inference with execution; simply refreshing more often does not help. In the NaVIDA ablation, 'Blocking w/ more rounds' roughly doubles rounds (9.75→18.50) but raises the waiting ratio from 30.5% to 52.2%. Full LiveVLN runs at a similar frequency (18.25 rounds) with only 10.3% waiting and 1.20 pauses. The two components do different jobs. Removing the revisable tail hurts task stability (R2R SR 59.9→57.6) and continuity (waiting 15.6%). Removing real-time latency-adaptive guard sizing leaves SR about the same (60.3) but raises waiting to 18.4% and pauses to 3.00. So the tail preserves adaptability and adaptive sizing preserves continuity. Episode-time savings stay moderate because physical execution time is unchanged.
method: Blocking-loop diagnosis and continuity metrics: episode time is decomposed as T_episode = T_execution + T_wait. Five client-side timestamps per round (send/recv/empty/issue/done) define inference latency, visible gap, resumed-step duration and interrupted-round duration. N_pause counts rounds with visible gap > 0.5 s.

Short-horizon action state q_t = [e_t | g_t | r_t]: executed actions since the last handoff, a released guard buffer held by the controller, and an unreleased revisable tail held by the inference thread.

Dual-thread guarded handoff: Thread A executes the guard g_t while Thread B computes the refreshed continuation û_{t+1} = D_B(o_{t+1}, g_t; r_t), conditioned on the committed guard and the newest observation. At handoff, g_t becomes executed, the refreshed prefix becomes the next guard, and the remainder stays revisable.

Real-time adaptation: an EMA estimates sense-and-inference latency, ℓ̃_{t+1} = (1-α)ℓ̃_t + αℓ_t, and the budget is ψ = ℓ̃ + δ. The next guard is the shortest prefix k* whose summed per-action execution-time estimates τ(a) cover ψ. The guard is sized in wall-clock time so it works for both primitives and macro-actions.
Safety fallback: if the background pass misses the deadline (ℓ_SI > T_guard), the controller emits a previously validated one-step backup action when it covers the overrun, otherwise STOP.

Backbone-specific instantiation: StreamVLN (4-action native continuation) uses a fixed 2-action guard on the robot, since one action ≈1.14 s and inference ≈0.52 s, and StreamVLN reuses its KV-cache. NaVIDA uses adaptive commitment of controller chunks, with τ estimated from empirical controller durations.

The paper does not explain how latency/asynchrony is emulated in the Habitat evaluation. The real-robot 'Stop within 2 m' metric is reported as counts (16/40, 12/40) and is placed in 'extra'.
results: On VLN-CE val-unseen, LiveVLN keeps benchmark performance close to the native checkpoints. StreamVLN† goes 56.4→57.2 SR on R2R and 54.4→53.7 on RxR; NaVIDA goes 61.4→59.9 SR on R2R and 57.4→56.7 on RxR. On a Unitree G1 humanoid it cuts average waiting time by 77.7% (StreamVLN, 7.32→1.63 s) and 72.8% (NaVIDA, 10.64→2.89 s). It lowers pause count (6.75→0.80 and 9.25→1.20) and visible gap (~1 s→~0.1 s). Wall-clock episode time falls 12.6% (41.98→36.71 s) and 19.6% (34.90→28.06 s), while stop-within-2 m success stays comparable.
limitations: Small task-success drop on NaVIDA (R2R SR 61.4→59.9, SPL 54.7→53.9). The simulation protocol for emulating streaming/latency is not described.
Real-robot evaluation is small: one office scene, 8 instructions × 5 repetitions, low absolute success (12–16/40), one humanoid platform over Wi-Fi to a remote GPU.

Requires navigators that emit multi-step autoregressive continuations conditioned on committed actions, plus hand-estimated action durations τ(a). StreamVLN uses a hand-fixed 2-action guard rather than the adaptive rule. Episode-time gains are bounded by physical execution time.
